en: Has God struck him down?
My troublesome father Manas
Has a tale that never ends.
Everywhere, to finish him,
Ruined peoples bear a grudge.
How can I know this calamity?
These many horses of my father, Khan Bakai—
Better for wretched me
To drive them toward the foothills.”
So saying, Baitailak,
Hurrying, stumbling in alarm,
Shouted out the news.
To all the wretched people,
He shouted, “Run!”
A horse-catching pole with a black loop,
He grasped it, spitting on his hands.
Furious and glowering,
The great, clattering herd of horses
He set about driving off in one rush.
Fat stallions and fat mares,
He chased and drove in a flurry.
Oh, that wretched Baitailak,
Crying the battle cry, ‘Bakai!’
The fat beasts that would not move,
He drove them all off in a flurry.
Behind him, mighty Bakai
Cried, “Baitailak!”
Baitailak, hurrying in alarm,
Drove them off all the harder.
Your elder, Lord Bakai,
Made his complaint to God:
“Better that I should die,
And see the face of Judgment!
Better that I should sink without begetting,
Than see a worthless son—
Better to pass away childless!
Like barren ground where no grass grows,
Better to be left without a field,
Without seeing offspring, wretched head,
Better that I should remain childless!
When I threw the whole world into turmoil,
And held it besieged,
When I raised a clamor through the six reaches,
And struck them down,
Why did I not die then?
Seeing nothing at all,
Why was I not barren?
Rather than see a worthless son,
Why did I not remain childless?
Alas, Tailak, stop a moment!
Woe, Tailak, stop a moment!
Worthless Tailak, stop a moment!
Swine Tailak, stop a moment!
Have you ruined my wealth?
You have run my horses to exhaustion.
You have badly drained my strength;
You have run my livestock to exhaustion.
Earth-bound Tailak, go into the earth!
Wretched Tailak, taken by God!
Alas, was Manas a lion?
Was Manas more of a warrior than I?
Kara-Shaar and Kambil—
This is the hand that besieged them!
Reducing the six reaches to ruin,
This is the hand that struck them!
Upon the face of the earth, turmoil—
I was Bakai who brought it.
Smashing every place I reached,
I was Bakai who conquered it.
I was Bakai who wore it.
Crushing many Chinese,
I was Bakai who drove them off.
Pinewood spear and cleaving steel,
I was Bakai who bound it on.
Looming like Opol Mountain,
I was Bakai who shone.
Saintly Sultan Manas's
Red banner with a golden crescent,
I was Bakai who held it.
Letting no enemy escape,
I was Bakai who slew them.
Alas, was Manas a warrior?
Alas, was my wretched life worth less than Manas's?
Look at Manas's son,
See how he comes!
But if you look at my son,
Always making trouble,
He is driving my horses away.
You have dug my pit deep,
Driving my horses off, beating them,
You have made my misery boil.
Making them call you Bakai's worthless son,
You have played a fine trick on me!”
So saying, mighty Bakai
Struck Kökcholok with his whip.
The black-sided heavy lash,
Leopard Bakai, the dear lion,
Seized and swung.
His worthless son Baitailak,
He struck upon the crown.
With no second stroke needed,
Leopard Bakai, the dear warrior,
Struck him down.
Five sets of nine, headed by a mare,
Warrior Bakai, the saint,
Had slaughtered when he arrived.
His worthless son Baitailak,
With no second stroke needed,
He struck him down now.
“My root has become stagnant water;
I have been left without a spring.
My dear head has been disgraced;
I have been left without offspring,”
So saying, lion Bakai,
With his orphan come at last,
Led him and showed the road,
Teaching what he did not know.
He would have him trace the path;
Bakai would show him wonders.
Khan Bakai's great court—
When the boy drew near,
Khan Bakai's Körpöyan
Came out before him, sobbing.
“The orphan left by my generous Manas!” she said.
She too wept, crying aloud:
“My precious one left by our dear friend,
My offspring left by the mighty one,
My dear one left by Manas, blessed by Khizir!
As the hair at my temples turns white,
As my journey lies before me this year,
When death comes and I must die,
When I must see the other world,
My precious orphan, have you come?
Have I, wretched soul, seen the orphan?”
Crying out, they greeted one another;
Crying out, they kissed one another.
Their Semetey had arrived;
The needed orphan was found.
There were more delights, more still.
Leopard Bakai, the fierce warrior,
Had tales told through the night.
For the orphan, Manas's son,
He slaughtered a yearling suckled by a barren mare,
Had him crunch sugar like snow,
Had him sip black tea,
Had him put aside every sorrow.
Fattened lamb, sweet head—
To entertain the boy as a guest,
He had the food boil vigorously.
Hosting him, slaughtering sheep,
He laid out his wealth equally,
Without looking high or low,
For the orphan seen only after mortal hardship,
He spared himself nothing.
His orphan had arrived at last;
His lion had been found upon the road.
The suffering orphan was found.
Now Khan Bakai prepared to travel,
Making ready toward his grandfather, the swine khan.
He taught what was unknown;
Such was the learned warrior Bakai.
He made the unperceived understood;
Such were the falcon's dark eyes.
Jar-Kiya of Jangirik,
A path for beasts in single file,
Whose hollow no man had scouted,
Where no one had traveled back and forth.
Elephants had been the beasts of burden.
Since Khan Bakai had last gone there,
Some twelve years had passed.
Now he saw that place.
“Oh, my dear colt,
This place here, Boz-Moinok—
When I see Boz-Moinok,
My heart stirs with memories of much play.
When I see this place,
My soul burns.
Between Talas and Keng-Kol,
A place whose worth the people knew,
Riding horses far, scouting the land,
Oh, my boy, loosing hounds and flying hawks,
Once, for Bakai,
That was the place of sport.
The rising foothill, the gray spur—
When my formidable Manas lived,
This elder of yours, Khan Bakai,
Kept watch and surveyed the land,
Went out on patrol and scouted the road.
That was your elder Khan Bakai's ridge.
For twelve full years,
Without loosing hounds or flying hawks,
I was that grief-stricken Bakai;
That was the place left empty.
And, my son Semetey,
Those rolling ridges there,
That land of rugged mountain passes,
The mottled pass standing apart—
When I see the land before me,
Tears pour from my eyes.
The rolling hills appear,
The rugged passes come into view.
Deer stream down from the hills;
The grass upon the hills grows sparse.
Ibex stream down from the terraces;
The grass upon the terraces grows sparse.
Wide passes, hills full of argali—
When I see that precious land,
I grieve, deep in thought.
When my sultan Manas lived,
This very Khan Bakai
Chased foxes from the open gullies,
And played all kinds of games there.
He chased argali from its hills;
From its hidden hollows, dear soul,
He shot its deer.
Its chervil grows thick as a forearm.
When its marals start and bolt,
They are like cows fleeing gadflies.
When I hunted in this place,
In those days of happiness,
Why did I not die then?
This place has patches of marsh,
With ducks and geese in separate flocks.
When Manas died,
My suffering grew heavy;
This land of mine was left desolate.
My heart is sorely troubled
When I see this place.
Your dear uncle Bakai
Sheds tears from his eyes.
When Manas died,
I forgot these pleasures;
This land of mine was left without a master.
Death did not come; I suffered,
Bereft of my Magnanimous One,
Unable even to die.
My Manas, gone long ago,
My Talas, left deserted!
The forty companions and six wicked ones
Since this land was left deserted,
Twelve years have passed.
Broad as a spreading tent,
My Manas's Kerme-Tash—
When I see this place,
My poor head fills with sorrow.
Below it lies a broad valley,
A valley complete in every way.
Plane trees as large as houses,
And house-sized towers reaching for the sky.
There is snow on the mountain side;
In its forests, my orphan,
Every living creature dwells.
When the nightingale sang from a plane tree,
No mortal could listen unmoved.
Those who bore sorrow sobbed,
And would not step a span outside it.
